title: Azure Cache for Redis Overview
description: Learn how Azure Cache for Redis improves application speed with in-memory caching, common caching patterns, and eviction policies.

data.text: A cache stores frequently accessed data in memory so applications can read it much faster than querying a database or making an external API call. Azure Cache for Redis is a fully managed in-memory cache service based on the popular open-source Redis engine. It reduces database load, lowers latency, and improves the overall responsiveness of your application.

data.title: Speed Comparison
data.text: A database query typically takes milliseconds to tens of milliseconds. A read from an in-memory cache like Redis often takes under one millisecond. Caching the right data can dramatically improve user-facing performance.

data.title: Available Service Tiers
items: Basic: a single node with no SLA, useful for development and testing.
Standard: a replicated cache with a high availability SLA and automatic failover.
Premium: adds clustering, persistence, virtual network support, and Redis Enterprise features.
Enterprise: full Redis Enterprise with active geo-replication and advanced modules like Redis on Flash.

data.text: Caching is not just about storing data. It is about deciding what to cache, when to refresh it, and what to do when the data is missing. Several well-known patterns help you use Redis effectively in real-world applications.

cards.title: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
cards.description: The application checks the cache first. On a miss, it loads data from the database, stores it in the cache, and returns it.
pros: Cache failures do not break the app

cards.title: Write-Through
cards.description: The application writes to the cache and the cache synchronously updates the database.
pros: Cache and database stay in sync
cons: Requires cache integration in write path

cards.title: Write-Behind (Write-Back)
cards.description: The application writes to the cache, and the cache queues updates to the database asynchronously.
cons: Risk of data loss if cache fails

cards.title: Refresh-Ahead
cards.description: The cache proactively refreshes popular items before they expire.
cons: May refresh items that are no longer needed

data.text: Redis is more than a simple key-value store. It supports rich data structures that make it useful for leaderboards, rate limiting, session management, and messaging. Understanding these data types helps you choose the right structure for your use case.

data.title: Core Redis Data Types
items: String: binary-safe text or binary data up to 512 MB.
Hash: maps between string field and value pairs, ideal for objects.
List: linked lists of strings, useful for queues and recent activity feeds.
Set: unordered collection of unique strings, great for tags and membership checks.
Sorted Set: a set where each member has a score, perfect for leaderboards and time-series data.
Bitmap: compact bit-level operations for flags and counts.
HyperLogLog: approximate counting of unique items with minimal memory.

data.title: Common Redis CLI Commands
data.content: Set, get, and expire a cache entry; add and retrieve items from a sorted set.
data.code:
# String operations
SET user:1001:session "eyJhbGciOi..." EX 3600
GET user:1001:session
DEL user:1001:session

# Hash operations for user objects
HSET user:1001 name "Alice" email "alice@example.com"
HGETALL user:1001

# Sorted set for leaderboard
ZADD leaderboard 1500 "player:1" 2300 "player:2"
ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES

data.text: When Redis reaches its memory limit, it must decide which data to remove to make room for new writes. The eviction policy controls this behavior. Choosing the right policy depends on whether you prefer predictability, cache hit rate, or data durability.

rows: Returns errors when memory is full
Databases where data loss is unacceptable
Removes least recently used keys across the entire dataset
Removes least recently used keys with an expire set
Mix of persistent and cache data
Removes least frequently used keys across the entire dataset
Skewed access patterns with some hot keys
Removes least frequently used keys with an expire set
Mix of persistent and cache data with skewed access

terms.definition: A read operation where the requested data is found in the cache, avoiding a slower database or API call.
A read operation where the requested data is not in the cache, requiring a fetch from the backing store.
Time To Live, the duration after which a cache entry expires and is removed.
The process of removing data from the cache when memory is full, governed by the configured eviction policy.

data.title: Design a Caching Strategy
data.description: You are adding caching to a product catalog API that serves product details by ID. Products are updated once per day and are read thousands of times per minute.
steps: Choose a caching pattern that fits read-heavy, infrequently updated data.
Set an appropriate TTL for product cache entries.
Select a Redis data type to store product details.
Explain how you would handle a product update event to keep the cache fresh.
data.expectedOutcome: You can describe a caching strategy using Cache-Aside with a daily TTL, and explain how to invalidate or update cache entries when product data changes.

data.title: Azure Cache for Redis Summary
points: Azure Cache for Redis is a fully managed in-memory cache based on Redis.
Standard and Premium tiers provide high availability and enterprise features.
Common patterns include Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead.
Redis data types include strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, and HyperLogLogs.
Eviction policies control which data is removed when memory is full.
data.takeaway: Azure Cache for Redis improves application performance by keeping frequently accessed data in memory, and its rich data types and eviction policies make it suitable for a wide range of caching scenarios.
